column4: The section’s ثور dictionary form describes an ox stirring earth as it searches with its legs; here the raven “يَبْحَثُ فِي الْأَرْضِ” and teaches how to “يُوَارِيَ” the body. Burial opens earth and then covers what it holds, the inverse of the section’s graves opened.
This repeats the section’s named بعثر root in “بُعْثِرَتْ” for graves overturned. It gives the same hidden grave contents a second, explicit Qur’anic staging.
“وَأَخْرَجَتِ الْأَرْضُ أَثْقَالَهَا” makes earth itself eject its burdens, a direct parallel to the section’s turned soil and “what is in the graves” brought out.
“أَلْقَتْ مَا فِيهَا وَتَخَلَّتْ” describes earth throwing out what is in it and emptying; this closely matches the section’s focus on the contents concealed in graves.

The section’s ثور dictionary entry names locusts taking flight as an eruption; here people stream from graves “كَأَنَّهُمْ جَرَادٌ مُّنتَشِرٌ,” making that secondary sense an explicit resurrection image.

The section’s ثور root is explicitly tied to plowing; “وَأَثَارُوا الْأَرْضَ وَعَمَرُوهَا” uses that root for turning and cultivating land. Its worldly building on worked earth sharpens the contrast with earth later opened to expose what it contains.
“مِنْهَا خَلَقْنَاكُمْ ... وَفِيهَا نُعِيدُكُمْ وَمِنْهَا نُخْرِجُكُمْ” gives the earth’s full cycle of origin, return, and renewed emergence that the section’s grave image stages at its end.

“يَبْعَثُ مَن فِي الْقُبُورِ” states that God raises those in graves. The section’s note that 100:9 says “what” is in graves rather than “who” makes this person-centered formulation a useful companion to its contents image.
“فَأَقْبَرَهُ” says God places the person in a grave, matching the section’s dictionary sense of qabr as the dead person’s resting place and the covered state that the later turning reverses.
“إِذَا شَاءَ أَنشَرَهُ” completes the preceding burial with God’s later raising of the person, the opening movement developed in the section’s “بعثر” image.
At the trumpet, people stream “مِنَ الْأَجْدَاثِ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِمْ يَنسِلُونَ”; this directly stages the emergence from graves that 100:9 describes as grave contents overturned.
“يَوْمَ تُبْلَى السَّرَائِرُ” names the testing and exposure of hidden secrets, closely matching the section’s account of what is in the breasts being extracted.
“لَا تَخْفَىٰ مِنكُمْ خَافِيَةٌ” says nothing about people remains hidden when they are presented, clarifying the section’s movement from concealed grave and breast contents to disclosure.

Immediately after 82:4 overturns the graves, this ayah says each soul knows what it sent ahead and left behind. It supplies the moral contents made visible by the upheaval, parallel to 100:10’s opened breasts.
The earth’s “زِلْزَالَهَا” is the convulsion that precedes the burdens’ emergence in 99:2, completing the ground upheaval named by that neighboring ayah.

After earth ejects its burdens in 99:2, “تُحَدِّثُ أَخْبَارَهَا” gives the earth a further act of disclosure: it reports its news. This extends the section’s image of the ground no longer keeping its contents hidden.

The awakened speakers ask “مَن بَعَثَنَا مِن مَرْقَدِنَا” (“who raised us from our resting place?”). That word for resting place echoes the section’s qabr dictionary sense, while their question voices the shock of the graves opening.

“مَا تَنقُصُ الْأَرْضُ مِنْهُمْ” says God knows what earth consumes from the dead and keeps it in a preserving record. The burial that hides or diminishes the body cannot erase the contents later brought out.

The section’s ثور dictionary form explains the ox through plowing earth; this cow is explicitly “لَا ذَلُولٌ تُثِيرُ الْأَرْضَ,” not trained to plow it. The negation marks the boundary of the source’s plowing sense.
The section shows graves opened at resurrection; here, after death, “بَرْزَخٌ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ يُبْعَثُونَ” sets a barrier until that day. It states the interval that bounds the opening scene.
“وَتَرَى الْأَرْضَ بَارِزَةً” depicts the earth laid bare as everyone is gathered, a broader version of the section’s soil turned over and hidden contents exposed.

After the earth is laid bare and all are gathered, the placed record “لَا يُغَادِرُ صَغِيرَةً وَلَا كَبِيرَةً” and shows what people did. It parallels the section’s extraction of breast contents by making no small or large item escape the accounting.
The section calls a grave the dead person’s resting place and hidden hollow; “أَلَمْ نَجْعَلِ الْأَرْضَ كِفَاتًا” extends that containing image from grave to earth.

This next ayah identifies the earth’s gathered contents as “أَحْيَاءً وَأَمْوَاتًا.” It completes 77:25’s receptacle image and clarifies how earth holds the dead whose contents the section sees turned out.

“أَنبَتَكُم مِّنَ الْأَرْضِ نَبَاتًا” pictures human life emerging from earth like growth. This parallels the section’s named ثور dictionary sense, “eruption of something,” and its movement from buried matter to emergence.
“يُعِيدُكُمْ فِيهَا وَيُخْرِجُكُمْ إِخْرَاجًا” completes the plant-from-earth image with return and extraction, a close account of the burial and re-emergence sequence.
The verse says God revives earth after its death and then “كَذَٰلِكَ النُّشُورُ.” This is a nonlexical parallel to the section’s hidden thing erupting from earth and the dead being brought out.

“يَمِيزَ الْخَبِيثَ مِنَ الطَّيِّبِ” describes separating bad from good. The section’s dictionary account of “تحصيل” as extracting precious metal from ore supplies a concrete sorting image for this moral distinction.

After the earth’s upheaval and report, this ayah says the one who did an atom’s weight of good “يَرَهُ.” It makes the disclosure fine-grained, like the section’s account of extracting and separating what was hidden.
This parallel continuation says the one who did an atom’s weight of evil “يَرَهُ.” The matching good-and-evil pair specifies what the exposure in 99:7 reveals.
When people ask their skins why they testified, the skins answer that God made them speak. The body’s own hidden witness is exposed, complementing the section’s extraction of what lies within.

“وَمَا كُنتُمْ تَسْتَتِرُونَ” recalls their attempt to hide from the testimony of hearing, sight, and skin, then says they wrongly thought God did not know much of their deeds. It reverses the section’s concealment root into failed concealment at disclosure.
“وَمَا تُخْفِي الصُّدُورُ” names what breasts conceal, matching the section’s image of extracting “what is in the breasts” and its discussion of the source section’s concealment sense under و ر ي.

The people “يَثْنُونَ صُدُورَهُمْ لِيَسْتَخْفُوا مِنْهُ” fold their breasts to hide, while God knows what they conceal. This gives a bodily concealment image that the section’s chest contents later overturn.
“مَا تُسِرُّونَ وَمَا تُعْلِنُونَ” and “بِذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ” join concealed and declared things to what is in breasts, the same hidden-to-exposed interior that the section develops.

“أَلْهَاكُمُ التَّكَاثُرُ” opens a sequence in which rivalry for more leads, in the next ayah, to visiting graves. This joins worldly accumulation to the section’s turn from intense love of wealth to grave contents brought out.

“زُرْتُمُ الْمَقَابِرَ” makes grave-visiting the endpoint of rivalry in accumulation. The visit by the living contrasts with the section’s graves opened and contents extracted, while the sequence links both to wealth.
“وَتُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا” gives an explicit parallel to Surah 100’s intense love of wealth, which immediately precedes the image of graves and inner contents exposed.

“دُكَّتِ الْأَرْضُ دَكًّا دَكًّا” follows the statement of intense love of wealth in 89:20. Its pounded earth pairs worldly wealth with the section’s upheaved ground and the judgment that uncovers what it held.
The person “جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ” accumulates and counts wealth, echoing Surah 100’s intense love of wealth before graves are opened and breast contents extracted.

The wealth collector “يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُ أَخْلَدَهُ” thinks his property will make him last forever. This is a sharp boundary against the section’s graves opened and inner contents exposed after the wealth-centered life.

This pictures people like “الْفَرَاشِ الْمَبْثُوثِ,” scattered moths, while the section’s ثور dictionary sense names locusts and 54:7 uses them for people streaming from graves. The insects differ, but both are specific swarm images for the final human gathering.
